lines.text: Do you know how fireworks get their colours? Every colour in the sky comes from a different metal, burning.
A firework shell is a paper ball. At the bottom, a lift charge of black powder fires it out of a tube, hundreds of meters up.
As it flies, a time fuse burns down inside. It's timed so the shell bursts right at the top.
Inside are pellets called stars, packed around a burst charge. When it explodes, the stars fly out, each one burning bright.
Their colour comes from metal salts. Heat kicks the metal's electrons up, and as they fall back, they give off light of one exact colour.
Strontium burns red. Barium, green. Copper, blue. Sodium, yellow. Blue is the hardest to make, because copper's colour fades when it gets too hot.
And the shape? That's just how the stars are packed. Arrange them in a ring, and the burst becomes a ring.
So every firework is chemistry, painted across the sky.
